ClusterSyn: Cell-Line-Specific Topology-Aware Drug-Combination Response Prediction on the O'Neil Dataset
abstract: Predicting cell-line-specific drug-combination response remains a central challenge in pharmacogenomics and precision oncology. In this study, we focus on the O'Neil drug-combination dataset because it has a distinctive and highly structured measurement topology: experimental compounds form a complete interaction core, originally FDA-approved drugs form a structurally unmeasured FDA-FDA block, and all experimental compounds are measured against all FDA-approved drugs. This design provides a natural setting to examine whether drug-interaction topology itself can serve as a predictive source of information. We introduce ClusterSyn, a topology-aware graph-based framework for drug-combination response prediction on the O'Neil dataset. ClusterSyn represents each cancer cell line as a weighted drug-interaction graph, preserving the shared measurement topology while allowing response scores to vary across cellular contexts. The method separates synergistic and antagonistic interaction structures, applies Markov clustering to identify local drug-interaction modules, extracts cluster-indexed graph-derived features, and integrates these signals through a modular ensemble regression model. ClusterSyn was evaluated using topology-preserving validation strategies, including leave-one-experimental-drug-out and leave-one-drug-pair-out designs. Across these settings, ClusterSyn achieved strong continuous response prediction performance and outperformed regression-based baseline methods on the primary error-based metric. Ablation and sensitivity analyses showed that local graph modularization, feature-family separation, and modular ensemble integration contributed to predictive performance. Additional analyses using Bliss Independence, Highest Single Agent, and Zero Interaction Potency scores showed consistent performance trends, indicating that the proposed graph-derived features were not limited to the Loewe Additivity Index. A regression-based case study selected 5-Fluorouracil as the lowest-error FDA-approved candidate and showed that its predictive performance remained stable across tissue, cancer-type, molecular-subtype, and individual cell-line contexts. Overall, ClusterSyn demonstrates that the structured measurement topology of the O'Neil dataset can provide useful graph-derived features for cell-line-specific drug-combination response prediction and candidate prioritization.

title: Drug combination prediction for cancer treatment using disease-specific drug response profiles and single-cell transcriptional signatures
abstract: <jats:p>Developing novel cancer treatments is a challenging task that can benefit from computational techniques matching transcriptional signatures to large-scale drug response data. Here, we present ‘retriever,’ a tool that extracts robust disease-specific transcrip-tional drug response profiles based on cellular response profiles to hundreds of compounds from the LINCS-L1000 project. We used retriever to extract transcriptional drug response signatures of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cell lines and combined these with a single-cell RNA-seq breast cancer atlas to predict drug combinations that antagonize TNBC-specific disease signatures. After systematically testing 152 drug response profiles and 11,476 drug combinations, we identified the combination of kinase inhibitors QL-XII-47 and GSK-690693 as the topmost promising candidate for TNBC treatment. Our new computational approach allows the identification of drugs and drug combinations targeting specific tumor cell types and subpopulations in individual patients. It is, therefore, highly suitable for the development of new personalized cancer treatment strategies.</jats:p>
